title: Every stone we could find
description: Two carved repertoires side by side: every openly licensed photograph of a Neolithic Anatolian and a Rapanui carved surface we could register, with what is legible on each.
deck: The comparison at the centre of this collection sets one Neolithic pillar beside one Pacific boulder. This page puts each of them back among its neighbours.
deck_2: Filter both walls at once. Nothing is removed — the stones that do not carry the feature stay on the wall, dimmed, because they are the reason the question is worth asking at all.
filter_note: Every count below describes the registered photographs, not the published corpus and not the objects. Several photographs may show the same surface, and an uncertain reading is never counted as a match.
anchor_note: These are the two carvings the Göbekli Tepe–Rapa Nui comparison actually rests on. Seen alone they are striking. The walls above are the context that decides how much that is worth.
context_note: Before a resemblance can cross an ocean it has to survive the question of why each side would produce it anyway. The two answers here are not symmetrical.
gap_note: Only dates already registered in this collection are drawn. An unresolved date cannot be plotted, and is listed below instead.
finding: That asymmetry is the result of the exercise. Birds are the dominant subject of the Rapanui carvings registered here and an occasional one among the Anatolian animals — and in this sample the Anatolian half of the comparison rests on a single stone, photographed three times. None of that decides whether the resemblance means anything. It does decide what the resemblance is between: not two bird-centred repertoires, but one pillar and a tradition.

review.reviewer: Deep Memory editorial / AI-assisted visual reading
review.note: Feature states are source-informed editorial readings of each registered photograph, prepared with AI; independent review is outstanding. “Legible” means the feature can be seen in that photograph. “Not legible in this view” is not a finding that the object lacks the feature, and this page cannot be used to argue that anything is absent.

selection.rule: Files were listed from fixed Wikimedia Commons categories for each tradition, before any of them were looked at. A file was kept if it is a photograph in which one carved or painted surface is the subject and legible enough to say what is and is not visible on it. Undecorated pillars were kept deliberately: they belong to the population the question is asked against.
selection.caveat: Photographic coverage is not corpus coverage. The published corpora are far larger than what Commons holds — Göbekli Tepe’s excavated pillars are catalogued by the excavation team, and the Orongo petroglyphs were surveyed in the standard Rapa Nui rock-art corpus. Neither total is reproduced here, so no frequency on this page is a frequency in either tradition.

selection.exclusion_note: Counts are of files listed, not of objects. Every photograph that survived the rule was then opened at full size and checked; eighteen were dropped at that stage, including a modern illustration of a bull, two annotated composites and eleven views of rock in which no carving could actually be read. The "further photographs" group is the honest reservoir: a second batch can register more surfaces without changing the rule.

corpora.label: Neolithic Anatolia
corpora.sites: Göbekli Tepe, Karahan Tepe and Nevalı Çori, with finds held in the Şanlıurfa museum.
corpora.context: The carved repertoire here is overwhelmingly animal: foxes, boars, aurochs, snakes, scorpions, spiders, leopards and cranes, arranged on and around T-shaped pillars that are themselves abstracted human bodies, with arms, hands and belts. Birds are one animal among many rather than the subject of the imagery, and no documented ritual explains the disc on Pillar 43. What the carvings meant is exactly what the excavators say remains open.

context_source.title: Pillar 43: of animals and a headless man
context_source.note: The excavation team’s own discussion of the animals and the competing readings of the disc.

corpora.label: Rapanui traditions
corpora.sites: Orongo and the wider island, with carvings held in the British Museum and other collections.
corpora.context: Rapa Nui has a documented reason to carve birdmen holding rounded forms. At Orongo, an annual competition sent servants to swim to the islet of Motu Nui and return with the first egg of the manutara, the sooty tern; the sponsor of the winner became the tangata manu, the birdman, for that year. The densest birdman carvings cluster at Mata Ngarau, the ceremonial outcrop above that competition. A bird beside an egg is the subject of the ritual itself.
